Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Initiation in HIV-Positive Individuals For adults and adolescents living with HIV, the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) at a CD4 count above 500 cells/mm³ compared to starting at a CD4 count of ≤500 cells/mm³ has been evaluated for its potential benefits and harms. The same question applies to children living with HIV. The outcomes assessed include mortality, progression to AIDS, tuberculosis (TB), non-AIDS events, treatment adherence, retention in care, viral suppression, severe treatment-related adverse events, and transmission of HIV, hepatitis C (HCV), and hepatitis B (HBV) in co-infected populations. For children, additional outcomes include immunological recovery, HIV drug resistance, TB incidence, and neurodevelopment. Sub-analyses consider age groups (adolescents aged 15–19 years, adults aged >19 years, and older adults >50 years) and specific populations, such as pregnant and postpartum women, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, sex workers, and HIV-positive partners in serodiscordant couples. 2013 WHO ART Guidelines The 2013 WHO guidelines recommended prioritizing ART initiation in individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. ART was also recommended for individuals with a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage. Additionally, ART initiation was advised for individuals with active TB, HIV/HBV co-infection with severe chronic liver disease, HIV-positive partners in serodiscordant couples, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, triple ART should be initiated and maintained at least for the duration of the risk of mother-to-child transmission. Women meeting treatment eligibility criteria should continue lifelong ART. In some countries, women not eligible for ART for their own health may discontinue ART after the risk of mother-to-child transmission has ceased. Evidence Supporting Early ART Initiation Since 2010, randomized controlled trials and observational studies have demonstrated that early ART initiation reduces HIV-related mortality, morbidity, disease progression, hospitalization, and transmission. It also decreases TB incidence and facilitates decentralization and task-shifting in healthcare systems. Current evidence strongly supports initiating ART at a CD4 count threshold of 500 cells/mm³, with a stronger gradient of effect at lower CD4 counts. Modeling projections and ecological studies suggest that very early ART initiation (regardless of or above 500 cells/mm³) can influence HIV incidence over time if testing, ART coverage, and retention are high at the population level. However, global HIV testing and ART coverage remain suboptimal, with late diagnosis and treatment initiation still common, even in high-income settings. Concerns about long-term safety, drug resistance, affordability, and sustainability of immediate ART initiation have been discussed. UNAIDS has proposed global 90-90-90 targets, aiming for 90% of people with HIV to know their status, 90% of those diagnosed to be on ART, and 90% of those on ART to achieve viral suppression by 2020. These targets aim to reduce AIDS-related deaths and new HIV infections to 500,000 annually. Research Evidence and Limitations A 2015 WHO systematic review and meta-analysis identified 18 eligible studies, including 17 observational studies and one randomized controlled trial (TEMPRANO-ANRS 12136). The outcomes evaluated included mortality, severe HIV disease, malignancy, clinical progression, AIDS events, non-AIDS events, TB, severe treatment-related adverse events, and HIV transmission. Data were pooled separately for randomized trials and cohort studies to estimate summary effect sizes. The evidence for initiating ART at CD4 counts ≥500 cells/mm³ is less robust than for starting at CD4 counts between 350 and 500 cells/mm³. Most data come from high-income settings, with limited representation from Africa and Asia. The TEMPRANO study in Côte d’Ivoire showed that immediate ART initiation plus six months of isoniazid preventive therapy significantly reduced severe HIV morbidity by 44% without increasing severe adverse events. The START study, conducted across 35 countries, demonstrated a 53% reduction in negative outcomes (death, AIDS, or serious non-AIDS events) with early ART initiation compared to deferred treatment. This effect was consistent across income and geographic regions. However, there is insufficient randomized trial data to support ART initiation at CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³ for population-level preventive benefits. Safety and Efficacy Considerations Preliminary data from the SEARCH study showed no significant differences in treatment retention, adverse events, or ART toxicity discontinuation between individuals initiating ART at CD4 >500 cells/mm³ and those starting at CD4 350–500 cells/mm³. High retention in care (>90%) and viral suppression rates (92%) were observed, including among those with CD4 >500 cells/mm³. Early ART initiation may improve immune restoration compared to treatment during chronic infection. Conclusion While early ART initiation offers significant benefits, including reduced morbidity and mortality, challenges remain regarding long-term safety, drug resistance, and programmatic feasibility. Further research is needed to address these concerns and optimize ART initiation strategies globally.
